messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 39
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 43

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Intrusive Memory: A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly, Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne, Expressions of Affection: Physical affection such as hugs
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Care: Seeking medical or psychological help, Avoid Religious Spaces: Places of worship or religious gatherings, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Leilani is a thirty-nine-year-old park ranger who grew up in a coastal village in Oceania before moving to the United States in her twenties. For nearly a decade, she worked as a relief coordinator for an international humanitarian organization, and it was during a deployment to a conflict zone that her life fractured. She had been assigned to a small medical outpost near a contested city, and one afternoon, as she helped unload supplies from a convoy, the compound was struck by mortar fire. In the chaos that followed, she found herself pinned beneath debris, unable to move, while a colleague beside her—a man named Tomas—was killed instantly. She remembers the smell of his cologne mixing with dust and smoke, and she remembers the way his body was lifted and thrown by the blast. What she cannot remember, no matter how hard she tries, is how she got out. There are gaps in her memory that feel like swallowed seconds—she cannot tell a clear story of what happened, even to herself. Some moments are agonizingly clear: the sound of the whistle before the mortar, the weight of the metal across her legs, the cologne. Others are blank, and when she tries to explain what happened to anyone, she loses the thread and cannot finish.

In the months after, Leilani left humanitarian work entirely and took a job as a park ranger in a quiet national forest, believing that open space and solitude would help her heal. Instead, the triggers followed her. The memory of the event comes to her mind suddenly, often without warning, and it is almost always brought on by the smell of a specific perfume or cologne—any scent that reminds her, even faintly, of Tomas. She has also found that physical affection, such as hugs from her husband, can set off the memory, because the closeness of another body reminds her of being pinned and helpless. Each time this happens, she feels the trauma surge back, and she has come to believe that she cannot trust her own mind. She believes she acted in ways that go against who she is—she had frozen, she had not been able to help Tomas, and she had survived when he did not—and this belief has grown into a deeper conviction that she no longer belongs anywhere, that her life is not worth living anymore. These negative appraisals make the triggers feel even more potent, because each intrusion confirms to her that she is broken and that she does not deserve to feel safe.

Leilani has developed a set of maladaptive strategies that she uses to manage the overwhelming fear. She avoids seeking medical or psychological help, because she is certain that talking about what happened will only make the gaps in her memory worse, and she avoids places of worship or religious gatherings, because the silence there reminds her of the stillness of Tomas's body. She is hypervigilant towards people, scanning every visitor to the park for signs of danger, and she has become acutely attuned to sudden movements by others, which put her immediately on guard. This hypervigilance, in turn, reinforces her memory problems, because when she is constantly scanning for threat, she cannot settle her mind enough to form a coherent narrative of what happened. The hypervigilance also triggers the memory itself, because a sudden movement can feel like the blast, and suddenly she is back in the compound. To manage this, she avoids unfamiliar places entirely, because she cannot assess the danger there, and she has stopped going to town for groceries, asking her husband to do the shopping instead. This avoidance has deepened her sense of isolation, and it reinforces her negative appraisals—she believes that her life is not worth living if she cannot even leave her own home.

The memory of the event, fragmented as it is, also drives her maladaptive strategies. Because she cannot tell a clear story, she has come to believe that if she tries to get help, she will not be able to explain herself, and so she avoids medical care entirely. The memory also triggers the negative appraisals, because when she tries to piece together what happened, she lands on the moment she froze, and she tells herself that she violated her own values. And the memory itself acts as a trigger, because the gaps in her mind feel like a kind of threat—she is afraid of what she might have done or not done during the blank seconds, and this fear brings the intrusive memory back more often. Her husband has noticed that she flinches when he hugs her, and he has stopped initiating affection, which makes Leilani feel even more disconnected. She has come to believe that she belongs nowhere, not even in her own marriage.

What finally brought Leilani to seek help was a moment in the forest last week. She was leading a group of schoolchildren on a guided walk, and one of the children ran toward her with sudden, excited movements. Leilani dropped to the ground, covering her head, and the children stared at her in silence. She could not explain what happened. She could not finish the sentence. That night, she told her husband that she was afraid of herself, and he made an appointment for her. She is most afraid that therapy will force her to remember the gaps, and that what she finds there will confirm that her life is not worth living. But she is also, quietly, hoping that someone can help her find a way back to the person she used to be.
